description: Aristotle analyzes Greek tragedy and coins words that are still everywhere: mimesis, catharsis, peripeteia. The Poetics is the first great instruction manual for storytelling.

hero.hook: Long before screenwriting manuals, there was Aristotle and Greek tragedy.

blocks.text: In the **4th century BC**, **Aristotle**, a student of Plato who became an independent thinker and founded the **Lyceum** in Athens, wrote the **Poetics**. It is not a poem. It is an analysis of poetry, and above all of **tragedy**, the Greek dramatic form that stages the fall of a hero. How does a story produce fear and pity? Why does that do us good?

The text that reached us is incomplete, sometimes dry, written down in the form of notes. Even so, it shaped theater, then the novel, then film. Many rules of “good storytelling” have their Greek ancestor here. Aristotle watches what works on stage, then draws principles from it.

Plato distrusted images, which he compared to deceptive shadows. Aristotle rehabilitates them through [[Aristotelian mimesis]]. For him, art imitates nature selectively. It shows things not as they are, but as they could be. Representing human actions is not lying. It is learning. A child imitates in order to understand. So does art.

blocks.caption: Aristotle: classifying the world, including the stories we tell ourselves

blocks.text: Tragedy imitates serious actions, complete and of a certain scale. The test is not documentary accuracy. It is the **probable** and the **necessary**: what had to happen in this story, given the internal logic of the plot. Aristotle also separates epic, a long narrative in verse, from tragedy, a stage action inside a limited span of time.

Aristotle says that tragedy achieves the [[catharsis]] of the emotions of pity and fear. The exact sense of the word has been argued over for twenty-five centuries: purification, purging, clarification? The central idea holds: a violent spectacle does not only excite us. It **orders** our feelings. We weep and shake in safety, inside the theater.

In the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, the text traveled through Arabic and Latin translations, including those linked to [[Averroes]], the Andalusian philosopher of the 12th century. Aristotle came back to Europe by scholarly detours, not in a straight line.

blocks.caption: The theater at Epidaurus: the space where a Greek city watched its own myths

blocks.text: For Aristotle, the heart of drama is the *muthos*, the plot, the chain of actions. He prizes **reversal**, the sudden turn of fortune, and **recognition**, the *anagnorisis*, the moment when a character moves from ignorance to knowledge. **Oedipus Rex** by Sophocles is his star example: the hero finds out too late who he is.

He prefers an **error**, the *hamartia*, an unintended fault or a warped judgment, to pure wickedness. The hero is neither perfectly good nor monstrous. His fall has to look logical, and that is what makes it terrible. The mixture is what produces pity: we recognize a human weakness, not just a cartoon villain.

French classicism in the 17th century, modern playwriting, Hollywood pitches: unity of action, the knot and the resolution turn up everywhere. You can dispute Aristotle. People still quote him. The [[Theatre of Epidaurus]], a Greek theater remarkable for its acoustics, is no longer the only home of storytelling, but the questions asked there remain.

Aristotle also reminds us that poetry speaks of the **general**, while history speaks of the **particular**. A well-built plot shows what could have happened, according to what is probable. That is why Oedipus remains a model: every revelation feels surprising and inevitable at once. Classical playwrights, and then modern screenwriters, took over this demand for narrative necessity.

The **Poetics** of Aristotle gave the West its first great vocabulary for storytelling: imitate, move the audience, reverse the situation. Before writing a story, many people still think it through with him.
